source.title_on_document: Effects of AI-generated images in visual art education on students' classroom engagement, self-efficacy and cognitive load

supplement.holds: The paper refers to no supplement. All statistics are in Tables 1-9 of the main text. Data availability statement (p. 12): no datasets were generated or analysed.

paper_design_summary: 78 fifth-grade students from two classes (39 each) at one primary school in Qingdao/Shandong, China, first learned a cartoon-painting task with classical (human-made) cartoon artworks. For a second task (draw an anthropomorphic cartoon character), the treatment group received teacher instruction illustrated with Stable Diffusion images made by a research assistant, while the control group received the same lesson illustrated with classical cartoon artworks. Students painted by hand; three teachers rated the task-2 paintings on five 1-5 rubric criteria, including creativity and originality. Engagement, self-efficacy and cognitive load were self-reported.

studies.label: Classroom experiment with fifth-graders (AI-generated vs classical example images, cartoon painting)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Treatment (GAI-assisted teaching with AI-generated example images) vs control (conventional teaching with classical artworks) for Task 2. The abstract says students were randomly assigned; the introduction calls the study quasi-experimental, and Methods says the participants came from two classes of 39 (the arm sizes), without saying whether individuals or classes were assigned.
assignment.quote: Seventy-eight fifth-grade students were randomly assigned to a treatment group (n = 39) and a control group (n = 39).
assignment.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 2, Introduction ('we conducted a quasi-experimental study involving 78 fifth-grade students, divided into control and treatment groups'); p. 4, Methods, Participants ('drawn from two classes: Class A (39 students) and Class B (39 students)')

arms.name: Treatment
arms.description: Task 2 taught with GAI-assisted method: teacher PowerPoint instruction using Stable Diffusion-generated anthropomorphic cartoon images (Fig. 3), then hand painting practice; interviews at post-test

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Task 2 taught with conventional method: same teacher, same lesson structure, instruction using classical artworks from iconic cartoon characters (Fig. 4), then hand painting practice

participants.exclusions: None stated; every table reports n = 39 per arm.
participants.who: Fifth-grade primary school students, ages 10-12 (mean 11.13, SD 0.437), 41 male and 37 female, from two classes
participants.quote: This study involved 78 fifth-grade students from a primary school in Shandong Province, China. The participants were drawn from two classes: Class A (39 students) and Class B (39 students), comprising 41 males and 37 females.

ai_tool.name_model: Stable Diffusion (checkpoints shown in Fig. 3: realvisxlV40_v40LightningBakedvae, AnythingXL_xl, cartoonArcadiaSDXLSD1_xenoArcadiaCX)
ai_tool.how_used: A research assistant generated cartoon images from structured prompts; the teacher used them as example artworks in the Task 2 PowerPoint instruction. Students did not use the AI tool themselves and painted with pencils, watercolours and paper (p. 6; p. 12, limitation 'Fourth').

task.description: Hand painting: 'Using the anthropomorphism techniques you have learned, create and design a distinct and characteristic anthropomorphic cartoon character.'
task.duration: Stage 3 (instruction plus painting practice) about 40 minutes (p. 6)

outcomes.name: Creativity and Originality (rubric score of Task 2 painting)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three teachers (two art teachers, one math teacher; Rater Z is also the course instructor) scored each painting 1-5 on 'How unique and imaginative is the artwork?'; raters reported blinded, artworks anonymized and randomized; ICC of composite across criteria 0.847. The label combines creativity and originality, so it could also be coded novelty.

contrasts.reported: Creativity and Originalit[y]: Treatment n = 39, mean 4.581, SD 0.444; Control n = 39, mean 4.205, SD 0.499; t = 3.515, p < 0.001

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is unclear on two counts. First, the abstract says students were randomly assigned, but the introduction calls the design quasi-experimental and Methods says the 78 students came from two intact classes of 39, the same size as each arm; the paper never says how assignment was done, so it may be two intact classes (one cluster per arm). Second, students never used generative AI: a research assistant generated example images that the teacher showed in instruction (AI role ideas_supplied), against human-made classical examples (ai_vs_active). Criterion 2: 78 people analyzed (39 + 39). Criterion 3: blinded teacher ratings of the paintings, including a 'Creativity and Originality' criterion. If the reviewer accepts the abstract's random-assignment claim and AI-generated examples as AI assistance, the study would qualify as field_rct; otherwise it is quasi_people context.

one_line_finding: Fifth-graders taught with Stable Diffusion example images scored higher than those taught with classical cartoon artworks on teacher-rated Creativity and Originality of their paintings (4.581, SD 0.444, vs 4.205, SD 0.499, n = 39 each; t = 3.515, p < 0.001) and on the other four rubric criteria (p. 11, Table 9).
open_questions: Were individuals or the two intact classes (Class A, Class B, 39 each) assigned to arms, and was the assignment random? The abstract says 'randomly assigned'; the introduction says 'quasi-experimental'.
Does showing AI-generated example images during teacher instruction (students never used the AI tool) count as generative-AI assistance for criterion 1?
Were the AI-generated images still visible while students painted? The paper places painting practice in the same Stage 3 lesson but does not say.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reports, not scored on the output: classroom engagement (four dimensions; Tables 3-4), self-efficacy (Tables 5-6), cognitive load (Table 7). Fig. 2 says Task 1 paintings were also rated at pre-test (Stage 2), but no Task 1 painting scores are reported, so there is no baseline for the painting outcomes. The p-values in Table 9 look one-tailed (t = 2.554 with 76 df gives two-tailed p of about 0.013); the paper does not say. Table 9 scores appear to be one per student (n = 39 per arm), presumably averaged over three raters; the paper does not state the aggregation. One rater (Rater Z) was also the course instructor, which weakens the stated blinding. Text and Table 4 disagree on the affective-engagement F (17.279 in text, 17.379 in table); this does not affect the creativity outcomes. The Methods says Data analysis also ran ANCOVA for paintings, but only t-tests are reported. ai_available_when_produced is coded yes because the paintings were made in the lesson that used the AI images; whether the images were visible during painting is not stated.
